attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his essay, stated in his own voice.

semantics.note: The normalised wording drops 'tangible' but keeps the substance: costly, compute-heavy models with no obvious mass-market use cases. It is a firm present-tense observation.

contract.note: Scoring the two clauses separately is fair. Counting a consumer support assistant used at large scale as a tangible mass-market use is an ordinary reading, though contestable. The window chosen to end at publication is reasonable. The verdict on the use-case clause turns on this reading.

evidence.note: A January 2024 survey calls computational and memory cost a big concern for LLMs. This supports the qualitative resource-burden clause only.

Klarna's own February 2024 announcement (a company disclosure, not independently checked) reports 2.3M conversations handling practical tasks such as refunds. Under the contract's reading, this contradicts the claim that no such use case existed.

reviews.rationale: The resource clause holds: contemporary research confirms heavy compute and memory costs. The use-case clause is contradicted under the contract's reading. Klarna's assistant was a deployed consumer service doing identifiable tasks at large scale before publication. That evidence is a company self-report, not independently validated. So the claim is partly supported and partly contradicted.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: The revision restores the qualifier 'does not appear' and the wording 'pretty terrible'. The second clause is stated without hedging.

contract.note: Separating actual replacement from announced cuts and from equivalent workload is fair. 'Large number' and 'pretty terrible' have no thresholds. The January–February 2024 window is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Only 383 US cuts were explicitly attributed to AI in January–February 2024, which is consistent with the first clause. But these are announcements, and Challenger says AI cuts may be filed under 'technological update'.
Klarna says its assistant matches human agents on satisfaction (company disclosure). This challenges a blanket 'terrible' verdict, but it does not show that workers were actually replaced.
A DPD chatbot failed in January 2024, but DPD still ran human service alongside it. This is not shown to be a case of AI replacing workers.

reviews.rationale: Announcement data suggests limited explicit AI-linked cuts, but it measures announcements, not completed replacements, and warns that AI cuts are under-attributed. No evidence pairs confirmed worker replacements with operational outcomes. Klarna's favourable self-report and DPD's failure each fall outside that frame. The packet does not settle either clause.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: An unqualified 'will' with 'eventually' is a scored forecast with no deadline. The normalised wording drops 'brutal' and softens 'any industry', which lowers the bar. The contract restores both.

contract.note: Requiring an adverse judgment, a broad reckoning, and a causal link between them is faithful to the compound forecast. The contract rightly says that elapsed time cannot disprove an 'eventually' forecast.

evidence.note: The Munich court's official release says it largely ruled against OpenAI on GEMA's copyright claims (November 2025, not yet final). This supports only the lawsuit-loss part of the forecast, not the reckoning.

reviews.rationale: An adverse but non-final copyright judgment against OpenAI exists. However, no evidence shows cross-industry restrictions or restructuring of model use caused by it. The early-resolution rule needs the full sequence, and the forecast has no deadline. It stays open.

attribution.note: These are Zitron's own words in his essay.

semantics.note: This is a firm categorical negative forecast with no deadline.

contract.note: The broad reading counts a roughly 90-second short, cut by humans from heavily curated clips at a 300:1 ratio, as Sora 'generating a movie'. That stretches the ordinary sense of movies against the speaker. In context he was dismissing film-making hype. The contract itself concedes that a feature-film reading is plausible and would give a different result.

evidence.note: Air Head is a completed short whose imagery all came from Sora, with heavy human editing and post-work. It contradicts only the stretched short-film reading.
A July 2026 filmmaker account says the Sora-backed Critterz feature was unfinished when OpenAI pulled Sora. No completed Sora feature is shown.

reviews.rationale: Under the contract's broad reading, Air Head would contradict the claim. That reading stretches 'movies' to include a brief, heavily human-assembled short. Under the ordinary feature-film reading, no Sora-generated movie was completed before Sora was withdrawn. But this open-ended negative has no deadline or conclusive rule. The result turns on an interpretation the speaker did not supply, so it is left unresolved.
